claim: The lateral septum (LS) is innervated by the hippocampus.
source: The lateral septum (LS), which is innervated by the hippocampus, is known to represent spatial information.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The lateral septum is known to represent spatial information.
source: The lateral septum (LS), which is innervated by the hippocampus, is known to represent spatial information.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Bezzi, 2005; Olton et al., 1978; Risold and Swanson, 1997; Wirtshafter and Wilson, 2019; Zhou et al., 1999).

claim: LS place cells are less numerous than in hippocampus.
source: While LS place cells are less numerous than in hippocampus, they are similar to the hippocampus in field size and number of fields per cell, but with field shape and center distributions that are more skewed toward reward.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing 75.2% (124/165) of CA1 cells versus 33.6% (127/378) of LS cells met the place field criteria.

claim: LS place cells are similar to hippocampus place cells in field size.
source: While LS place cells are less numerous than in hippocampus, they are similar to the hippocampus in field size and number of fields per cell, but with field shape and center distributions that are more skewed toward reward.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing average CA1 place field length of 29.1±14.7 cm versus LS place field length of 28.8±16.6 cm with no significant difference.

claim: LS place cells are similar to hippocampus place cells in number of fields per cell.
source: While LS place cells are less numerous than in hippocampus, they are similar to the hippocampus in field size and number of fields per cell, but with field shape and center distributions that are more skewed toward reward.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing the distributions of field numbers were not significantly different between CA1 and LS cells.

claim: LS place cell field shape and center distributions are more skewed toward reward compared to hippocampus.
source: While LS place cells are less numerous than in hippocampus, they are similar to the hippocampus in field size and number of fields per cell, but with field shape and center distributions that are more skewed toward reward.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing LS had significantly more place fields in choice arms (41.1% vs 29.2%) and different skew patterns.

claim: Spike cross-correlations between hippocampus and LS are greatest for cells that have reward-proximate place fields.
source: Spike cross-correlations between the hippocampus and LS are greatest for cells that have reward-proximate place fields, suggesting a role for the LS in relaying task-relevant hippocampal spatial information to downstream areas, such as the VTA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing place cell pairs with fields in the choice side had significantly higher mean average correlation than pairs with fields in the middle or forced arm.

claim: The LS has a role in relaying task-relevant hippocampal spatial information to downstream areas, such as the VTA.
source: Spike cross-correlations between the hippocampus and LS are greatest for cells that have reward-proximate place fields, suggesting a role for the LS in relaying task-relevant hippocampal spatial information to downstream areas, such as the VTA.
evidence: This is suggested based on the inference from the cross-correlation data and anatomical connectivity.

claim: The lateral septum is innervated by all CA fields of the hippocampus.
source: The lateral septum (LS), which is innervated by all CA fields of the hippocampus, contains place cells, and processes spatial information received from the hippocampus (Bezzi, 2005; Olton et al., 1978; Risold and Swanson, 1997; Wirtshafter and Wilson, 2019; Zhou et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The lateral septum contains place cells.
source: The lateral septum (LS), which is innervated by all CA fields of the hippocampus, contains place cells, and processes spatial information received from the hippocampus (Bezzi, 2005; Olton et al., 1978; Risold and Swanson, 1997; Wirtshafter and Wilson, 2019; Zhou et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations and demonstrated by the experimental data.

claim: The lateral septum processes spatial information received from the hippocampus.
source: The lateral septum (LS), which is innervated by all CA fields of the hippocampus, contains place cells, and processes spatial information received from the hippocampus (Bezzi, 2005; Olton et al., 1978; Risold and Swanson, 1997; Wirtshafter and Wilson, 2019; Zhou et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Spatial information from the hippocampus is hypothesized to be sent to downstream areas such as the hypothalamus and ventral tegmental area (VTA) for use in reinforcement and reward seeking.
source: It has been hypothesized that this spatial information is sent to downstream areas, such as the hypothalamus and ventral tegmental area (VTA) for use in reinforcement and reward seeking (Jiang et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2011; Swanson et al., 1981; Sweeney and Yang, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The LS has been implicated in contextual reward seeking.
source: The LS has also been implicated in contextual reward seeking and the formation of conditioned place preferences (Jiang et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The LS has been implicated in the formation of conditioned place preferences.
source: The LS has also been implicated in contextual reward seeking and the formation of conditioned place preferences (Jiang et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Little is known about the septal representation of space during reward seeking.
source: However, little is known about the septal representation of space during reward seeking and what, if any, transformation place information undergoes from its representation in the hippocampus to the lateral septum remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: What transformation place information undergoes from its representation in the hippocampus to the lateral septum remains unknown.
source: However, little is known about the septal representation of space during reward seeking and what, if any, transformation place information undergoes from its representation in the hippocampus to the lateral septum remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: CA fields of the hippocampus contain place cells that show preferential firing when an animal traverses a specific location, the 'place field'.
source: The CA fields of the hippocampus contain place cells that show preferential firing when an animal traverses a specific location, the 'place field' (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Spatially specific firing has been well documented and characterized in the entorhinal cortex.
source: Spatially specific firing has also been well documented and characterized in other brain areas, including in the entorhinal cortex (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005; Quirk et al., 1992), where this firing is believed to play a role in path integration (Fyhn et al., 2007; Knierim et al., 2014; Monaco et al., 2011; Moser et al., 2008), and in the lateral septum (Bezzi et al., 2002; Kita et al., 1995; Leutgeb and Mizumori, 2002; Monaco et al., 2019; Takamura et al., 2006; Wirtshafter and Wilson, 2019; Zhou et al., 1999), though much less is known about the potential role of LS place fields in spatial navigation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Spatially specific firing in the entorhinal cortex is believed to play a role in path integration.
source: Spatially specific firing has also been well documented and characterized in other brain areas, including in the entorhinal cortex (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005; Quirk et al., 1992), where this firing is believed to play a role in path integration (Fyhn et al., 2007; Knierim et al., 2014; Monaco et al., 2011; Moser et al., 2008), and in the lateral septum (Bezzi et al., 2002; Kita et al., 1995; Leutgeb and Mizumori, 2002; Monaco et al., 2019; Takamura et al., 2006; Wirtshafter and Wilson, 2019; Zhou et al., 1999), though much less is known about the potential role of LS place fields in spatial navigation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Spatially specific firing has been documented in the lateral septum.
source: Spatially specific firing has also been well documented and characterized in other brain areas, including in the entorhinal cortex (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005; Quirk et al., 1992), where this firing is believed to play a role in path integration (Fyhn et al., 2007; Knierim et al., 2014; Monaco et al., 2011; Moser et al., 2008), and in the lateral septum (Bezzi et al., 2002; Kita et al., 1995; Leutgeb and Mizumori, 2002; Monaco et al., 2019; Takamura et al., 2006; Wirtshafter and Wilson, 2019; Zhou et al., 1999), though much less is known about the potential role of LS place fields in spatial navigation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: The LS is anatomically located between areas involved in spatial navigation such as the hippocampus, and reward/reinforcement related areas such as the VTA.
source: Given the anatomical location of the LS between areas involved in spatial navigation such as the hippocampus, and reward/reinforcement related areas such as the VTA (Luo et al., 2011; Risold and Swanson, 1997), and the established role of the LS in reinforcement seeking (Jiang et al., 2018; Mathieu-Kia et al., 1998; McGlinchey and Aston-Jones, 2018; Olds and Milner, 1954; Oshima and Katayama, 2010; Sotomayor et al., 2005), we hypothesized that LS place fields would be preferentially located at reward locations to a greater extent than hippocampal place fields and contain more reward related information.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The LS has an established role in reinforcement seeking.
source: Given the anatomical location of the LS between areas involved in spatial navigation such as the hippocampus, and reward/reinforcement related areas such as the VTA (Luo et al., 2011; Risold and Swanson, 1997), and the established role of the LS in reinforcement seeking (Jiang et al., 2018; Mathieu-Kia et al., 1998; McGlinchey and Aston-Jones, 2018; Olds and Milner, 1954; Oshima and Katayama, 2010; Sotomayor et al., 2005), we hypothesized that LS place fields would be preferentially located at reward locations to a greater extent than hippocampal place fields and contain more reward related information.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The authors hypothesized that LS place fields would be preferentially located at reward locations to a greater extent than hippocampal place fields.
source: Given the anatomical location of the LS between areas involved in spatial navigation such as the hippocampus, and reward/reinforcement related areas such as the VTA (Luo et al., 2011; Risold and Swanson, 1997), and the established role of the LS in reinforcement seeking (Jiang et al., 2018; Mathieu-Kia et al., 1998; McGlinchey and Aston-Jones, 2018; Olds and Milner, 1954; Oshima and Katayama, 2010; Sotomayor et al., 2005), we hypothesized that LS place fields would be preferentially located at reward locations to a greater extent than hippocampal place fields and contain more reward related information.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: The authors hypothesized that LS place fields would contain more reward related information than hippocampal place fields.
source: Given the anatomical location of the LS between areas involved in spatial navigation such as the hippocampus, and reward/reinforcement related areas such as the VTA (Luo et al., 2011; Risold and Swanson, 1997), and the established role of the LS in reinforcement seeking (Jiang et al., 2018; Mathieu-Kia et al., 1998; McGlinchey and Aston-Jones, 2018; Olds and Milner, 1954; Oshima and Katayama, 2010; Sotomayor et al., 2005), we hypothesized that LS place fields would be preferentially located at reward locations to a greater extent than hippocampal place fields and contain more reward related information.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: The authors simultaneously recorded cells from the hippocampal CA1 field and the caudodorsal lateral septum during a spatial navigation task.
source: In the following experiment, we simultaneously recorded cells from the hippocampal CA1 field and the caudodorsal lateral septum during a spatial navigation task.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The caudodorsal LS was chosen as it is the area of the LS most heavily innervated by the hippocampus.
source: The caudodorsal LS was chosen as it is the area of the LS most heavily innervated by the hippocampus and known to send the most projections to the VTA (Luo et al., 2011; Risold and Swanson, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The caudodorsal LS is known to send the most projections to the VTA.
source: The caudodorsal LS was chosen as it is the area of the LS most heavily innervated by the hippocampus and known to send the most projections to the VTA (Luo et al., 2011; Risold and Swanson, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The lateral septum contains a large number of place cells with fields that have properties similar to the place cells of the hippocampus, including similar field size and similar number of fields per cell.
source: We found that, although not as common as in the hippocampus, the lateral septum contains a large number of place cells with fields that have properties similar to the place cells of the hippocampus, including similar field size and similar number of fields per cell.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of findings and supported by data in the results section.

claim: LS cells are slightly less accurately spatially tuned compared to HPC place cells.
source: However, in contrast to HPC place cells, LS cells are slightly less accurately spatially tuned.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of findings and supported by data showing LS cells have slightly but significantly less accuracy than HPC cells.

claim: Within a firing field, LS cells ramped up their firing in the direction of reward.
source: Additionally, within a firing field, LS cells ramped up their firing in the direction of reward, and place fields in the lateral septum were preferentially biased toward reward locations compared to the hippocampus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of findings and supported by data on skew patterns.

claim: Place fields in the lateral septum were preferentially biased toward reward locations compared to the hippocampus.
source: Additionally, within a firing field, LS cells ramped up their firing in the direction of reward, and place fields in the lateral septum were preferentially biased toward reward locations compared to the hippocampus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of findings and supported by data showing LS had significantly more place fields in choice arms.

claim: HPC and LS cells with reward proximate fields had significantly higher correlated activity than cells with fields located further from reward.
source: We found that HPC and LS cells with reward proximate fields had significantly higher correlated activity than cells with fields located further from reward.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of findings and supported by cross-correlation data.

claim: Reward-related spatial information from the hippocampus is preferentially represented in the LS.
source: We suggest that reward-related spatial information from the hippocampus is preferentially represented in the LS, and we provide three models by which this could occur.
evidence: This is suggested based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Relayed information from the hippocampus to the LS is used downstream to direct the animal to significant or rewarded locations.
source: We suggest that this relayed information is used downstream to direct the animal to significant or rewarded locations.
evidence: This is suggested based on inference from the experimental data and anatomical connectivity.

claim: The authors recorded the activity of 452 caudodorsal LS units and 178 CA1 hippocampus units in six male Long Evans rats.
source: In order to characterize the role of the LS in reward-driven spatial navigation, we recorded the activity of 452 caudodorsal LS units and 178 CA1 hippocampus units in six male Long Evans rats (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a description of the experimental data.

claim: The caudodorsal LS receives a large innervation from the hippocampus.
source: We specifically targeted the caudodorsal LS as it receives the a large innervation from the hippocampus and is the primary source of LS projections to the VTA (Luo et al., 2011; Risold and Swanson, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The caudodorsal LS is the primary source of LS projections to the VTA.
source: We specifically targeted the caudodorsal LS as it receives the a large innervation from the hippocampus and is the primary source of LS projections to the VTA (Luo et al., 2011; Risold and Swanson, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: 75.2% (124/165) of CA1 cells met or exceeded the 0.8 bits/spike threshold.
source: We found that 75.2% (124/165) of CA1 cells (Figure 2A) and 33.6% (127/378) of LS cells (Figure 2B) met or exceeded the 0.8bits/spike threshold, with the average bits/spike of a CA1 cell significantly higher than the average bits/spike of an LS cell (HPC mean 1.54+−1.2 bits/spike, LS mean 0.73+−0.7 bits/spike, two-tailed two sample t-test t(541)=9.42, p<0.001) (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 33.6% (127/378) of LS cells met or exceeded the 0.8 bits/spike threshold.
source: We found that 75.2% (124/165) of CA1 cells (Figure 2A) and 33.6% (127/378) of LS cells (Figure 2B) met or exceeded the 0.8bits/spike threshold, with the average bits/spike of a CA1 cell significantly higher than the average bits/spike of an LS cell (HPC mean 1.54+−1.2 bits/spike, LS mean 0.73+−0.7 bits/spike, two-tailed two sample t-test t(541)=9.42, p<0.001) (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The average bits/spike of a CA1 cell is significantly higher than the average bits/spike of an LS cell (HPC mean 1.54±1.2 bits/spike, LS mean 0.73±0.7 bits/spike, two-tailed two sample t-test t(541)=9.42, p<0.001).
source: We found that 75.2% (124/165) of CA1 cells (Figure 2A) and 33.6% (127/378) of LS cells (Figure 2B) met or exceeded the 0.8bits/spike threshold, with the average bits/spike of a CA1 cell significantly higher than the average bits/spike of an LS cell (HPC mean 1.54+−1.2 bits/spike, LS mean 0.73+−0.7 bits/spike, two-tailed two sample t-test t(541)=9.42, p<0.001) (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The distribution of the bits/spike for artificial LS units was highly significantly different than the distribution of bits/spike for actual units (KS test, p<10−15).
source: The distribution of the bits/spike for the artificial units was highly significantly different than the distribution of bits/spike for actual units (KS test, p<10−15), and only 7.96% of artificial units had bits/spike measurements of greater than 0.8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results.

claim: Only 7.96% of artificial LS units had bits/spike measurements of greater than 0.8.

claim: The average bits/spike for artificial LS units was 0.43, compared to an average value of 0.73 for actual units (two-tailed two sample t-test, t(818)=6.72, p<10−10).
source: The average bits/spike for the artificial units was 0.43, compared to an average value of 0.73 for actual units (two-tailed two sample t-test, t(818)=6.72, p<10−10).

claim: CA1 units had a mean of 1.34±1.4 bits/sec, and LS cells had a mean 0.82±1.1 bits/sec.
source: We found a mean of 1.34+−1.4bits/sec for CA1 cells, and 0.82+−1.1bits/sec for LS cells (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Units in the hippocampus had a significantly greater mean bits/sec than in the LS (two-tailed two sample t-test t(541)=4.57, p<0.001).
source: Units in the hippocampus had a significantly greater mean bits/sec than in the LS (two-tailed two sample t-test t(541)=4.57, p<0.001) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results and supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Of the 164 HPC units with bits/spike greater than or equal to 0.8, 104 units had at least one place field.
source: Of the 164 HPC units with bits/spike greater than or equal to 0.8, 104 units had at least one place field, with 63 of these cells with one field, 33 with two fields, seven with three fields, and a single cell with four fields (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Of the 127 LS cells with bits/spike greater than 0.8, 100 had at least one place field.
source: Of the 127 LS cells with bits/spike greater than 0.8, 100 had at least one place field, with 54 with one field, 33 with two fields, six with three fields, five with four fields, and two with five fields (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B,D.

claim: The distributions of field numbers were not significantly different between CA1 and LS cells (two sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test, p>0.5).
source: The distributions of field numbers were not significantly different between CA1 and LS cells (two sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test, p>0.5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results.

claim: Very little spatial firing in LS cells could be explained by correlations with speed or acceleration (median r2 value of 0.06).
source: Only two cells with place fields had an r2 of >0.5, with the median r2 value of 0.06 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), so very little spatial firing could be explained by correlations with speed or acceleration.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Out of 165 recorded CA1 cells that met spike rate and track coverage criteria, 104 (63.0%) met or exceeded a bits per spike cut off of 0.8 and had at least one place field.
source: In summary, out of 165 recorded CA1 cells that met spike rate and track coverage criteria, 104 (63.0%) met or exceeded a bits per spike cut off of 0.8 and had at least one place field that met the described criteria, while out of 378 recorded LS cells meeting spike rate and track coverage criteria, 100 (26.5%) met the same criteria (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for additional place cell examples and representations of firing rates).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of the data.

claim: Out of 378 recorded LS cells meeting spike rate and track coverage criteria, 100 (26.5%) met or exceeded a bits per spike cut off of 0.8 and had at least one place field.
source: In summary, out of 165 recorded CA1 cells that met spike rate and track coverage criteria, 104 (63.0%) met or exceeded a bits per spike cut off of 0.8 and had at least one place field that met the described criteria, while out of 378 recorded LS cells meeting spike rate and track coverage criteria, 100 (26.5%) met the same criteria (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for additional place cell examples and representations of firing rates).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of the data.

claim: Place cells in the CA1 are significantly more abundant than in the cdLS (two-tailed two sample t-test t(541)=8.6, p<0.001).
source: Place cells in the CA1 are therefore significantly more abundant than in the cdLS (two-tailed two sample t-test t(541)=8.6, p<0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results.

claim: The average length of a CA1 place field was 29.1±14.7 cm.
source: The average length of a CA1 place field was 29.1+−14.7 cm (Figure 4A,C), while the average length of an LS place field was 28.8+−16.6 cm (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: The average length of an LS place field was 28.8±16.6 cm.
source: The average length of a CA1 place field was 29.1+−14.7 cm (Figure 4A,C), while the average length of an LS place field was 28.8+−16.6 cm (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4B,D.

claim: The average field lengths in CA1 and LS were not significantly different (two-tailed two sample t-test t(320)=-0.16, p>0.05).
source: The average field lengths were not significantly different (two-tailed two sample t-test t(320)=-0.16, p>0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results.

claim: Both the hippocampus and LS had highly accurate place fields starting with the first pass of the place field.
source: Both the hippocampus (Figure 4E) and LS (Figure 4F) had highly accurate place fields starting with the first pass of the place field, though, on average the HPC is slightly more accurate on the first lap as well as across all laps.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Fields in both the HPC and the LS significantly increase firing in their place field with experience on the track.
source: Fields in both the HPC and the LS significantly increase firing in their place field with experience on the track (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: When travelling toward a reward site, cells in the hippocampus were skewed positively toward the direction of travel.
source: We found that, when travelling toward a reward site, cells in the hippocampus were skewed positively toward the direction of travel, while, when traveling away from a reward site, cells were skewed negatively away from the direction of travel, and this difference was significant (two-tailed two sample t-test t(207)=-2.1, p<0.05) (Figure 5A,B, see also Figure 5—figure supplement 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results and supported by data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: When traveling away from a reward site, hippocampal cells were skewed negatively away from the direction of travel, and this difference was significant (two-tailed two sample t-test t(207)=-2.1, p<0.05).
source: We found that, when travelling toward a reward site, cells in the hippocampus were skewed positively toward the direction of travel, while, when traveling away from a reward site, cells were skewed negatively away from the direction of travel, and this difference was significant (two-tailed two sample t-test t(207)=-2.1, p<0.05) (Figure 5A,B, see also Figure 5—figure supplement 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results and supported by data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: When traveling toward a reward site, LS place fields were skewed negatively away from the direction of travel.
source: Conversely, when traveling toward a reward site, LS place fields were skewed negatively away from the direction of travel, and when traveling away from a reward site, the fields were skewed positively toward the direction of travel, though this difference is not significant (two-tailed two sample t-test t(246)=-1.7, p=0.09) (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: When traveling away from a reward site, LS place fields were skewed positively toward the direction of travel, though this difference is not significant (two-tailed two sample t-test t(246)=-1.7, p=0.09).
source: Conversely, when traveling toward a reward site, LS place fields were skewed negatively away from the direction of travel, and when traveling away from a reward site, the fields were skewed positively toward the direction of travel, though this difference is not significant (two-tailed two sample t-test t(246)=-1.7, p=0.09) (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results and supported by data shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: There was no significant difference for values of skew based on whether a place cell was uni or bi directional in both HPC and LS (both two-tailed two sample t-tests, p>0.05).
source: Although the HPC and LS both contains uni- and bi- directional place fields, there was no significant difference for values of skew based on whether a place cell was uni or bi directional (both two-tailed two sample t-tests, p>0.05, see Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is a highly significant relationship between skew and FRAI values in HPC and LS cells.
source: Because skew can be sensitive to changes in speed, we also computed the firing rate asymmetry index (FRAI, see methods) (Mehta et al., 2000) for HPC and LS cells, and found a highly significant relationship between skew and FRAI values (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), showing that skew cannot be explained by the animal's speed.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Skew cannot be explained by the animal's speed.
source: Because skew can be sensitive to changes in speed, we also computed the firing rate asymmetry index (FRAI, see methods) (Mehta et al., 2000) for HPC and LS cells, and found a highly significant relationship between skew and FRAI values (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), showing that skew cannot be explained by the animal's speed.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the relationship between skew and FRAI.

claim: Skew values were not significantly different for hippocampus traveling to and from reward (two sample two sided t-test, t(74)=-0.59 p>0.05).
source: Skew values were not significantly different for hippocampus traveling to and from reward (two sample two sided t-test, t(74)=-0.59 p>0.05), but were significantly different for LS cells to and from reward (two sample two sided t-test, t(108)=-2.10, p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical test results.

claim: Skew values were significantly different for LS cells traveling to and from reward (two sample two sided t-test, t(108)=-2.10, p<0.05).
